utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, this is case number IT-01-42/2-I, the Prosecutor versus Vladimir Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. May I have the appearances, Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel. For the Prosecution, Susan Somers, senior trial attorney; also present, Mr. Phillip Weiner, trial attorney; Mr. David Re, trial attorney; Mr. Aleksander Kontic, legal advisor; and Mr. Sebastiaan van Hooydonk, case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you Ms. Somers. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, and my dear colleagues. For the accused Vladimir Kovacevic, Tanja Radosavljevic as counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Radosavljevic. We have called this hearing because the Chamber finds itself in a situation where we have to make further examinations as how to proceed, and I think there are two aspects of it. The first one is the medical aspect because it's the mental condition of the accused that is at the basis of the problems we are facing in the proceedings. We are also confronted with a situation where there are reports contradicting each other in their conclusions as to the fitness of the accused to enter a plea and the fitness of the accused to stand trial. So that's the first issue we'd like to concentrate upon. Then of course the next issue is whether, based on the findings we'll make in this respect, how to proceed, what are what our options are and which option to choose. Before we start, I'd first like to ask the parties whether they received the most recent report from the hospital in Belgrade where the accused is treated at this moment. That is a report dated the 30th of March, 2005. As a matter of fact, the cover letter is dated the 30th of March, and the report itself is the -- dated the 29th of March. Have you received that? Ms. Radosavljevic, did you also receive that?

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are aware that the Chamber has taken steps to seek the assistance of an expert to see whether these experts could assist the Chamber in better evaluating and better understanding the difference in the assessment of the present mental condition of the accused. I would suggest that we first hear this expert of which he has not sent any written report but have the parties received his curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, we -- counsel, Defence counsel and I did meet yesterday and discussed actually this -- the order that came out yesterday. It was only yesterday that both parties became aware of the appointment of this individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it was lately filed. I do agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Even the fact that the -- Your Honour had -- sought the assistance so we are only -- we have only the Dutch version of a CV, we have no translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I speak some Dutch. If there are any questions in relation to that CV, I would be, although not an official translator, and I'm aware that knowing a language and being a professional interpreter or translator is quite different. But if there would be any problem, we will try to assist in solving that. Ms. Radosavljevic, did you also receive the curriculum.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did and as well as my colleagues from the OTP. It is in Dutch so we will have to rely on your assistance in that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From what I can read from it, apart from that -- this expert, Mr. -- Dr. Duits is on the list of experts that is kept by the Registry that it at least shows a considerable experience, especially in forensic psychiatry. You see that at least publications are -- I just go briefly through it. Dr. Duits was educated, he studied medicine until 1988 at Amsterdam University. He became a psychiatrist, psychotherapist in 1994 and he got that degree at the -- also at the Free University, which is also a University in Amsterdam, and 1995 is mentioned as a youth psychiatrist, also University of Amsterdam. Then his experience, he reported on from 1989 in civil and criminal or -- I should say penal cases before courts. In 1991, he became an expert at the Court of Appeal in Amsterdam; that means that he's listed as such. On from 1990, he has functioned on the forensic psychiatry service of the Ministry of Justice. On from 2000, it says that he is listed as a rappoteur for the ICTY, and from 1996 until present, senior rappoteur supervisor, and educating other rappoteurs researching on quality of reporting. He worked as an assistant psychiatrist in one of the Dutch penitentiary institutions from 1988 until 1990. From 1993 to 1998, he was a psychiatrist in various penitentiary institutions. From 1997 to 2003, he was a psychiatric consultant for the council for the youths, that's an institution in the Netherlands under the supervision of the Ministry of Justice which deals with youth care. Since 2000, he was for Youth Forensic Psychiatry Services working in Amsterdam and since June 2002, he is the main responsible person for which is abbreviated as FPD, Youth Netherlands, and as far as I understand, FPD understands for forensic psychiatric services. That's in short, at least, the experience. And apart from that, you see the usual lists of where he has taught, about his publications, symposia he attended, and addressed which organisation he is a member of, et cetera. That's the -- I would say the usual lists. If this informs the parties sufficiently, I'd like to proceed. I'd like to hear Dr. Duits in private session, since I take it that details of the psychiatric history and details of the present psychiatric diagnosis may be necessary to be discussed. So therefore I suggest to the parties we do that in private session whereas we would then return into open session if we will consider what options we, at least in the view of the parties, we would have to proceed. Is there any objection against private session for the psychiatric part?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just address the Court. I note that in -- when actually the case -- the only other case that's gone to full hearing in this institution which is the Prosecutor versus Pavle Strugar had a full competency hearing which involved a number of things that might traditionally have been considered private session. It was conducted in open session because the idea was that the public would have an interest in all aspects underlying fitness which would include treatment issues as well as diagnosis issues. If the Chamber has in fact ruled on it, we respect the ruling, but I wanted to make the Chamber aware of the fact that all aspects of that hearing last April, I believe it was, were in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From what I remember from the Strugar case, it is that the physical health condition was mainly the issue whereas any mental condition was what one would normally expect from people at a higher age, whereas the mental condition to be discussed here would be at least quite different from what there was in Strugar. But let's first ask Ms. Radosavljevic what the position of the Defence would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The Defence would prefer to have this part of the discussion which will mention not only the diagnosis but everything else connected to the mental state of my client in private session, the same as we did on the 15th of March 2004 where we talked about the details of his diagnosis and his illness in a private session. And afterwards, the conclusions which are - I agree with you - of public interest, we discussed in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If we can reach any conclusions at this moment, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The -- having heard the parties and in view of the observations made especially in -- and not only the observations made in respect of the -- I would say the -- the intensive medical report we could expect, which is more than the usual and rather superficial medical issues, also in view of the history of this case, and also in comparison with the Strugar case leads the Chamber to decide that we'll hear the psychiatric part in private session. Madam Registrar, could we turn it to private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are back in open session, although perhaps not for very long. I'd like to ask Madam Usher to escort Mr. Duits into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Duits, good afternoon. Madam Usher asked you to stand. Although the rules are not perfectly clear on oral submissions by experts, I'd like you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, which may sound a bit unfamiliar to you as a Dutch expert, because under Dutch law, as I happen to know, there's a different formulation for experts compared to witnesses. But I hope you'll understand that it has exactly the same meaning, that you as an expert should give your opinion to the best of your abilities on the basis of your experience and whatever additional facts are known to you that you speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. On that, I explained this to you because I'm aware of our formulation, a bit different from what you are used to. Madam Usher will now give the text of the solemn declaration to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please be seated, Dr. Duits. Dr. Duits, I addressed you in English. I -- may I take it that your knowledge of the English language is such that you'll understand and that you'll -- you are able to express yourself in English and if there be any problem in respect of that, please address the Court so that we could try to find a solution for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Dr. Duits, we'll soon turn into private session since the Chamber has decided that the mental condition of the accused contains so much information which should be private and should not be made public but I first of all would like to draw your attention to what the Court asks you to do as it is mentioned in a request this Chamber addressed to the Registry to appoint an expert. We sought the assistance of a forensic medical expert to review the reports, mainly the last reports, presented on the medical condition of Mr. Kovacevic and we split it up in three parts, to provide the Chamber with oral submissions -- oral observations concerning the scope and the nature of the discrepancies between the expert report of Drs. Goreta and Krajinovic filed on the 20th of January, 2005, and the expert report of Dr. Rosic filed on the 22nd of March, 2005. That was the first part. Second, to provide oral observations as to how to solve the discrepancies between those two reports, and, third, to provide any other observation which could assist the Chamber in evaluating these reports. And you will understand we have to evaluate these reports since the Chamber will have to decide whether Mr. Kovacevic is fit to enter a plea and whether he is fit to stand trial. I wanted to explain this in open court why this Chamber has asked you to assist us and I'd now like to turn into private session so we can hear your observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be brought in, the expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Duits, I left a question with you. At the same time, I have to inform you, although I really regret it, that we are under some time pressure as well. This is not to hurry up you to an extent unacceptable but it's just to see whether we can be as efficient as possible. Please, tell us whether that question brings you to any further observations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, you have to, and -- and I cite, of course, from the reports, that he has a narcissistic personality disorder, narcissistic traits, and that means that you have ideas of curiosity, inflated self esteem, and you see also from the reports of the hospital, from the military academy, that he wants an exclusive position. That gives a lot of trouble for the hospital. Now, if he is -- in a certain way, he has this exclusive position when he comes to the Court in Den Haag, if he has to be trialed [sic] in Serbia-Montenegro in his home language with the same rights and no exclusive position in a psychiatric ward with other people, it might give big problems to keep his self esteem at [indiscernible] logical heights and if -- if you look to the facts, what does he have left? Pensioner? Threat of a trial, and now they are trialed [sic] in front of and between his own people, no exclusive rights anymore. That might, I'm speculating now, but you asked me to do that, I think, that might, yeah, heighten the risk of self -- suicidal ideation might be more pronounced if that has to be decided. But I said in the beginning, suicidal threat, suicidal ideation stays in whatever context, and it's, in fact, a prisoner's dilemma and I can't answer about that, in fact. Here he has an exclusive position. Over there, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Radosavljevic, do you have any questions for Dr. Duits?

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honours, I have a number of questions and I'm afraid that it will take at least half an hour to go through those questions, anticipating that the answers won't be too long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I take it, Ms. Somers, that you would have some questions as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think under the present circumstances, we would rather concentrate on when we could continue this hearing because we might not finish today. Dr. Duits, I don't know if you have any plans to go on a long holiday or whether your agenda would allow a return on a rather short notice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't like it because I have a full agenda but what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither do we.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first consult the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar now tries to find out whether there is any opening in the court schedule which, of course, doesn't mean that we could fit that in because we have all our agendas but, Dr. Duits, if I tell you that initial appearances now take place at 8.00 in the morning because we have no courtrooms available at other times and no Chambers, then you'll understand that it's the same everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while there's some discussion there, originally when this was scheduled, given we had notified Chambers of some scheduling issues from the Prosecution side, it was thought that perhaps if we needed a second day, either -- that Monday may be an option. Is that still an option? I think I had indicated to your senior -- to Mr. Harhoff that there would be some limitation from here and the proposal, as I understood it, was if we spilled over, there might be either a possibility of another day this week to finish the spillover or Monday, the 18th. Is that still the situation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll try to find out. At the same time, let's try to use our time as good as possible. Perhaps -- wouldn't it be fair, Ms. Radosavljevic, unless your questions are so related, that I give you the opportunity to put one or two questions, I do the same thing for the Prosecution and that meanwhile Madam Registrar tries to find out whether we have the option to continue on short notice and then ask also the witness. Could I give you that opportunity to start with.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: First question I actually would like to ask you is in regards with the way you saw the two reports, one is from the 20th of January by Dr. Goreta and Krajinovic and the other one is I think the 22nd of March by Dr. Rosic. You saw some -- in a formal way, you saw some differences on the matter -- in the matter on formal side of those reports. Could it be that considering that both Dr. Goreta and Dr. Krajinovic come from the same, let's say, legal system in terms of forensic expertise as you do, on one hand, it's the European continental system, and Dr. Rosic comes from another system from New Zealand where, actually, they apply something like the UK law, the law of the United Kingdom, so could that be the reason why she didn't maybe formally put her report in the way that you would see it as proper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The formal aspects of report writing in the English-speaking part, U.K., Australia, New Zealand, and USA, they refer to the same material as we do here also. I -- it's my research subject, in fact, and the Dutch Board of Psychiatrists has the same format of report writing as the USA, American Board of Psychiatrists, and you can find these aspects in this report writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that one. The other question that I would like to ask you, also more general question, besides of -- of the last reports also considering the additional reports of Dr. Goreta and Dr. Krajinovic and the reports of the military medical hospital in Belgrade, have you seen any other medical documents of Mr. Kovacevic? I also notice that you mentioned Dr. Strikovic because so you also read his report from May 203, May 2003, sorry, what about his previous records

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've rea the -- I've had the clinical observations of Dr. Petrovic, I have the military medical academy, I have also a report of the Defence from Dusan Kosovic [phoen] and I don't have the report of Mr. Strikovic, only that it's cited in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: So I presume that you also don't have the reports or rather medical documents in regards of Mr. Kovacevic seeking treatment which began in 1988.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's -- no, no. That's cited in the reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. There is one question that was raised by the Trial Chamber, and it actually refers to -- to the term delusional disorder. Now, if I could just cite you from a psychiatric book, or rather synopsis, I will tell you in a moment also the title of it and the authors.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kaplan and Sadock.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yup.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as to the confusion on the terminology and you of course will correct me if I'm wrong, because I'm -- I'm not a psychiatrist, it's on page 503 of synopsis of psychiatry, behavioural science, clinical psychiatry, and the authors are Kaplan, Sadock, and Grebb. It is also an annex to the Defence submissions from 31st March. It says under delusional disorder, "delusional disorder is defined as a psychiatric disorder in which the predominantly symptoms are delusions. Delusional disorder was formerly called paranoia or paranoid disorder." So do we -- can we see the delusional disorder that Dr. Rosic refers to in her report as the paranoid psychosis that was mentioned in the Goreta reports -- the Goreta-Krajinovic reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, the delusional disorder is -- doesn't appear that often. It's also mentioned in Kaplan and Sadock. It's a circumspect disorder which lasts very long, it's difficult to treat and I couldn't find the arguments in the report of Dr. Rosic to state that there is a delusional disorder. But did I answer your question, no? What did you ask me? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The question was if delusional disorder or as it was previously known, paranoia or paranoid disorder, can we see it as the same illness or mental disease that it is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. No. Delusional -- no. Paranoid psychosis, which is difficult to circumscribe [sic] but has also hallucinations with it sometimes, and delusions. And delusional disorder is strictly delusional.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The time is up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not entirely, because we are working hard on how to continue, but Ms. Somers, if you would like to put a few questions or the most important questions to start with, we could start, if you say if we have to restart any how, I'll do that at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If, in fact, as Dr. Goreta's report suggests that there may be as it come, potential from manipulation and couldn't this be true of any person facing charges in a criminal arena.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well I can only talk about a diagnostic, psychiatric diagnostic point of view. You have always, bear in mind, as a diagnostician, that malingering plays -- assimilation plays a part in the people you have before you. Yup.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And if in fact, there was some improvement but always a threat of regression and an individual aware of it, could that not frustrate the entire criminal justice system, if someone could be okay as long as you don't take me to trial. Can you imagine any rule of law, society, that could allow that potential for manipulation or that, perhaps, failure to treat so as to allow that in a situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, before the witness answer that question, I'd like to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Duits, the Chamber is inclined to take it that answering this question would be beyond your expertise. If you would have a different view, we had alike to hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's -- I was already looking to you if I had to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The potential for a trial or for the relationship of an accused in his home or national jurisdiction such as, let's say, Serbia, how would you view the fact that he may have hero status there with respect to his self esteem as opposed to accused status, given what is widely reported in the press about a number of accused before this Tribunal being considered heroes in their national jurisdictions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a good remark. I can't -- in fact, it's also beyond my expertise, in fact, but it doesn't -- it isn't mentioned in the report, but it could be possible that that has to do with his self esteem, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The number of reports that you have read, have you noticed the diagnosis of delusional disorder in any of them other than Dr. Rosic's?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I would have more questions but they would require more time so if the Court will indulge us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we should now look at Madam Registrar. I think all the court scheduling has changed but of course we'll first try to find out what the options are not only for us, Dr. Duits, but also what the options for you would be. Madam Registrar, could you inform us, and I noticed that you changed already a lot. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The only day that's available in the coming weeks is the afternoon of Tuesday, the 19th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I regret when I informed my colleague, Mr. Harhoff that that is one day that I am not available. If it, in fact, has to be within the next two weeks it's a problem for me either -- other team members but any time after the 3rd of May is ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will not be available after the 3rd of May and we can't give it too much time so although I was informed about it from Mr. Harhoff that at least onward from that date you would not be available anymore, that there is -- well, we have taken at into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: My colleagues with handle it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Duits, could I, because you are most vital in such a position, could I ask you if there would be any chance that you would be available on the 19th of April in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the late afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would make no problem, I suggest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could be here at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you've got one moment because I've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Duits, you were about to make a suggestion as far as the time is concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can make it at 5.00, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At 5.00. Yes, usually court hearings here can continue until 7.00, so 5.00 would not be a problem and we should be -- it should be possible. Then we'll deal with it. Then, Ms. Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The 19th of April, 5.00 is okay with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Ms. Somers, the -- someone to replace you could be found for that specific moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Replace never, but substitute yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I should be -- I should mind my words, I'm aware of that. Finally, I have got two short issues. Your presence are needed but it -- take a couple of minutes, so if you would prefer to leave, then please say so then I'll ask Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom. If not ... Ms. Radosavljevic, you've seen in the scheduling order for this hearing and I should have addressed the matter at the beginning and not halfway, that the Chamber didn't consider the presence of the accused necessary. I take it that since you appear here alone and that we did not receive any submission urging us to have the accused transferred from Belgrade, that you would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, to the extent there's -- instructed by your client, but of course the whole issue is about instructions and so therefore, we have to be practical. Then I have another matter. One of the others items on the agenda is, apart from what we should decide on the issue of fitness to enter a plea, yes or no, then, of course, we would have the next step and it is how to proceed in the case. I just give you a few options the Chamber might consider and perhaps the parties are invited to already give it some thought on how they would -- how their position would be in view of that option. First option would be to take another six months and see how matters develop and not to insist on entering a plea at this moment, not take any decision in that respect. Then the next option would be that if we would decide that it's now the time to determine whether a plea could be entered or not be entered, so that's to say no six -- no further six months but we'll take a decision now, then we have one possibility that is that the witness would -- that the accused would enter a plea, that our decision would be that we require him to enter a plea and if he doesn't do it, it will be done on his behalf. Then we have, after that, at this moment, I'm not on the basis of the material we have, I'm not considering the option although it is an option, of course, that if the accused will be invited to enter a plea, it would be a guilty plea but on the basis of what we've read now, I would make that at this moment a theoretically still existing possibility, but not something to be specifically considered by the parties at this moment. So if he would enter a plea, then the next question would be whether he would -- if he has entered a plea of not guilty or if such a plea is entered on his behalf, whether he would stand trial in The Hague or whether he would stand trial at another place. That might be Belgrade, if the Referral Chamber would follow the suggestion made by the Prosecution. That decision is beyond the competence of this Chamber because whether or not the case, after a plea has been entered, would be referred or not be referred to the former Yugoslavia is within the exclusive competence of the Referral Chamber. Then, the next option would be that the Chamber would decide now, so not take another six months and say that the witness -- the accused is not fit to enter a plea or not fit to stand trial. Then I think there are a few options. One of them, as far as I understand, supported at this moment by the Office of the Prosecution is that nevertheless, the application for a referral under 11 bis could be heard by the Referral Chamber, and I already point at the issue that would then most likely arise, which is the following: If someone is declared by this Chamber not to be fit to enter a plea or not to be fit to stand trial, then the next question would be whether he would be fit to instruct counsel as to represent him in any 11 bis proceedings. I'm not giving an answer to that question, I would just like the parties to consider that. Then, finally, that's the last option that comes into the mind of the Chamber at this moment, that is that the Prosecution would decide to withdraw the indictment which, of course, also is an option and the Chamber could imagine that if an indictment would be withdrawn, it could be just done as the French say, sec, that is without any further arrangements. Another possibility might be that a decision on the withdrawal of an indictment would be taken after consultation with local authorities, most likely would that be authorities this Belgrade, whether they would further monitor the health situation, and they might be willing to initiate Prosecutions, perhaps after consultation with the OTP once the situation is such that it would be appropriate to further proceed against this accused. These are the options that at least came into the mind of the Chamber. Since we will discuss these matters, the Chamber thought it wise to inform you about that so that you could, of course, prepare other options as well, but at least consider these or at least let it go through your minds when we resume. Dr. Duits, I would first of all like to thank you for coming and also for being available next week. Final -- the final confirmation, because you will understand we need a lot of people to come together here, it's -- we now know of the parties, the registry, Judges, and not less important, from you, but there are a few other matters to be considered as well. We'll confirm it to you at the shortest notice. Madam Registrar, is there any other matter we would have to raise at this moment? If not, we'll adjourn until Tuesday, the 22nd of -- the 19th of April, 5.00 in the afternoon, in courtroom -- that would be in Courtroom II. We adjourn.
